title: Small Farms, Large Stakes
text:
In many developing countries, the typical farm is small: a few acres, cultivated by a family that eats part of what it grows and sells the rest. For much of the twentieth century, such farms were often regarded as a relic, destined to be replaced by large and mechanised estates. Today, many development economists take a more respectful view. Small farms, they point out, frequently produce as much per acre as larger ones, and sometimes more, because families work their own land with great care and use labour intensively.

The obstacles small farmers face lie less in the size of their plots than in the conditions surrounding them. A farmer without secure title to his land has little reason to invest in improving it, and cannot offer it as security for a loan. Without credit, he cannot buy better seed or fertiliser at the start of the season, and may be forced to sell his harvest immediately at a low price to repay debts, rather than storing it until prices recover. Poor roads raise the cost of reaching markets, while limited information leaves him dependent on intermediaries who know the prices better than he does.

Each of these problems has a remedy, and none requires the small farm to disappear. Clear and secure land records encourage investment. Rural roads and storage facilities allow farmers to choose when and where to sell. Extension services, which bring practical advice on seeds, soil and water to the field, can spread improved methods quickly. Farmers’ cooperatives allow many small producers to buy inputs and sell produce in bulk, gaining some of the bargaining power that large estates enjoy.

Because so many of the world’s poor live in rural areas and depend on agriculture, improving the lot of small farmers is among the most direct ways of reducing poverty. It is also, in an age of uncertain food supplies, a matter of national interest.

title: What Is Lost, and Found, in Translation
text:
It is often said that something is always lost in translation, and the saying is true as far as it goes. The sound and rhythm of a poem, the play on words that depends on a particular language, the associations a word carries for native speakers: these rarely survive the journey intact. A translator who renders every word faithfully may produce a text that is accurate and lifeless; one who pursues the spirit of the original may be accused of taking liberties.

Yet the emphasis on loss can obscure how much translation makes possible. Most readers encounter the great works of other cultures, whether ancient philosophy, sacred texts or modern novels, only through translation. Entire traditions of thought have been transmitted in this way, as scholars in one age and language rendered the works of another into their own, often adding commentary that became influential in its own right. Without translators, the intellectual history of the world would be a collection of isolated rooms.

Translation also changes the language that receives it. In searching for equivalents, translators coin new words, borrow others and bend familiar structures to accommodate unfamiliar ideas. Over time these innovations can enrich the receiving language, giving it resources for expression it did not previously possess. A language that has translated widely is, in a sense, a language that has travelled.

Perhaps the best way to think of translation, then, is not as a copy that inevitably falls short of an original, but as an act of interpretation, even of creation. Every translation reflects choices about what matters most in a text, and no two translators will make exactly the same ones. This is why great works are translated again and again: each generation finds in them something its predecessors missed, and needs new words to say it.

title: Why Cities Run Hot
text:
On a summer evening, a person driving from the countryside into a large city may notice the air growing warmer as the buildings close in. The effect is not imagined. Cities are often noticeably hotter than the surrounding countryside, particularly at night, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island.

Several causes combine to produce it. Concrete, asphalt and brick absorb a great deal of the sun’s energy during the day and release it slowly after dark, keeping the air warm long after sunset. In the countryside, by contrast, plants and moist soil use part of the sun’s energy to evaporate water, a process that cools their surroundings. Cities replace much of this vegetation with hard, dry surfaces. Tall buildings trap heat between them and reduce the wind that might carry it away, while vehicles, air-conditioners and factories add heat of their own.

The consequences go beyond discomfort. Hot nights prevent the body from recovering from the heat of the day, and during heatwaves the elderly, the sick and those who work outdoors are especially vulnerable. Higher temperatures increase the demand for cooling, which raises electricity consumption and, where power comes from burning fuel, adds to pollution. There is an unhappy circularity here: air-conditioners cool the rooms they serve while releasing yet more heat into the streets outside.

Fortunately, the urban heat island is among the more tractable environmental problems, because its causes lie in choices about how cities are built. Planting trees along streets provides shade and cooling through evaporation. Roofs and pavements made of lighter-coloured materials reflect more sunlight instead of absorbing it. Parks, green roofs and open water bring some of the countryside’s cooling back into the city. None of these measures is costly in comparison with the damage that unchecked urban heat can do, and many bring other benefits, from cleaner air to more pleasant streets.

title: When the Machine Decides
text:
Decisions that were once made by people are increasingly shaped by automated systems. Software helps to decide who receives a loan, which job applications are read by a human being, and which neighbourhoods receive more attention from inspectors. Supporters of such systems argue, with some justice, that they can be faster and more consistent than human officials, who are prone to fatigue, prejudice and whim.

Consistency, however, is not the same as fairness. An automated system learns from past data, and if past decisions reflected unfair treatment of certain groups, the system may reproduce that pattern while giving it an appearance of scientific neutrality. Because the reasoning of complex systems can be difficult even for their designers to explain, an applicant who is refused may never learn why, and may have no practical means of challenging the result.

This raises a pressing question of accountability. When a human official makes an unjust decision, we know whom to hold responsible. When a decision emerges from a system designed by one company, trained on data collected by another and deployed by a public agency, responsibility is easily diffused until no one appears to bear it. Each party can point to the others, and the person harmed is left with no one to answer.

The answer is not to reject automation, which can bring real benefits, but to insist that responsibility cannot be delegated to a machine. The institution that uses a system must answer for its decisions as if a human official had made them. People affected by important decisions should be told when an automated system has been involved, given an intelligible reason, and offered a route to have the decision reviewed by a person. Systems should be tested regularly for unfair outcomes before and after they are introduced. Technology can assist judgement; it should never become a way of escaping it.

subject: English
q: The best title for the passage would be:
o: The Inevitable Rise of Large Estates
Why Farmers Distrust Cooperatives
The Mechanisation of Agriculture
Supporting the Small Farmer
explanation: The passage argues that small farms are productive, identifies the conditions that hold them back, and proposes remedies that do not require them to disappear.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why do small farms often produce as much per acre as larger ones?
o: They receive more fertiliser from the government
Families work their own land carefully and use labour intensively
They occupy the most fertile land
They use more machinery than large estates
explanation: The first paragraph attributes their productivity to families who ‘work their own land with great care and use labour intensively’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a farmer who lacks credit may be forced to:
o: sell his harvest immediately at a low price
store his harvest until prices recover
join a cooperative against his will
give up the title to his land
explanation: The second paragraph says that without credit he ‘may be forced to sell his harvest immediately at a low price to repay debts, rather than storing it until prices recover’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘relic’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: a sacred object
a profitable investment
something surviving from an earlier time
a new invention
explanation: Small farms were seen as ‘a relic, destined to be replaced’ by modern estates — a leftover from the past, not a sacred object.

subject: English
q: The passage implies that intermediaries can profit at the farmer’s expense because they:
o: own the roads leading to the markets
know market prices better than the farmer does
run the government’s extension services
issue the farmers’ land titles
explanation: Limited information leaves the farmer ‘dependent on intermediaries who know the prices better than he does’, an imbalance they can exploit when buying his crop.

subject: English
q: Which of the following statements would the author most likely reject?
o: Cooperatives can give small producers greater bargaining power
Rural roads help farmers choose when and where to sell
Helping small farmers is a direct way of reducing poverty
Development requires small farms to be replaced by large mechanised estates
explanation: The author presents the view of small farms as a relic as outdated and insists that ‘none [of the remedies] requires the small farm to disappear’; the other statements are made in the passage.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best states the central idea of the passage?
o: Translation should be avoided because it distorts the original
Although translation involves loss, it is also a creative act that transmits and enriches culture
Only poetry loses its meaning in translation
Translators should always render every word literally
explanation: The author accepts that something is lost but argues that translation carries ideas between cultures, enriches languages and is best seen as ‘an act of interpretation, even of creation’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a translator who renders every word faithfully may produce a text that is:
o: free but inaccurate
beautiful but misleading
obscure but profound
accurate but lifeless
explanation: The first paragraph says such a translator ‘may produce a text that is accurate and lifeless’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, how does translation affect the language that receives it?
o: It can enrich the language with new words and structures
It makes the language simpler and poorer
It replaces the language’s grammar with a foreign one
It has no lasting effect on the language
explanation: The third paragraph says translators coin and borrow words and bend structures, and that ‘over time these innovations can enrich the receiving language’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘liberties’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: political rights
holidays from work
unwarranted freedoms with the original
careful precautions
explanation: A translator who pursues the spirit rather than the words ‘may be accused of taking liberties’ — of departing too freely from the original text.

subject: English
q: With which of the following would the author most likely agree?
o: A perfect translation reproduces every feature of the original
Translation is a mechanical task requiring no judgement
Two competent translations of the same work may legitimately differ
Languages that borrow foreign words are weakened by them
explanation: The last paragraph says every translation reflects choices ‘and no two translators will make exactly the same ones’, treating such differences as natural rather than as errors.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred from the passage that great works are translated repeatedly because:
o: each generation interprets them afresh and needs its own words to do so
earlier translations are always inaccurate
publishers wish to sell more copies
the original languages have been forgotten
explanation: The final sentence explains that ‘each generation finds in them something its predecessors missed, and needs new words to say it’; it does not claim earlier versions were simply wrong.

subject: English
q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: the benefits of air-conditioning in modern cities
the history of city planning
the effects of climate change on the countryside
the causes and effects of urban heat and the ways it can be reduced
explanation: The passage defines the urban heat island, explains its causes, describes its consequences and ends with practical remedies.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, one reason the countryside stays cooler than the city is that:
o: it receives less sunlight than the city
plants and moist soil use part of the sun’s energy to evaporate water
its buildings are made of darker materials
it has more vehicles and factories
explanation: The second paragraph explains that in the countryside ‘plants and moist soil use part of the sun’s energy to evaporate water, a process that cools their surroundings’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why are hot nights particularly harmful?
o: They prevent the body from recovering from the heat of the day
They increase the number of vehicles on the roads
They stop plants from evaporating water
They make tall buildings absorb more sunlight
explanation: The third paragraph states that ‘hot nights prevent the body from recovering from the heat of the day’, which endangers vulnerable people during heatwaves.

subject: English
q: The word ‘tractable’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: impossible to measure
widely ignored
capable of being managed or solved
rapidly worsening
explanation: The problem is called ‘among the more tractable’ because its causes lie in building choices, and the author then lists affordable remedies — it can be dealt with.

subject: English
q: The ‘unhappy circularity’ mentioned by the author refers to the fact that:
o: cities grow larger as they become hotter
the means used to escape the heat add to the heat outdoors
trees planted in cities die in the heat
heatwaves return at the same time every year
explanation: The author explains that air-conditioners ‘cool the rooms they serve while releasing yet more heat into the streets outside’, so the response to heat worsens it.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards solving the problem of urban heat is best described as:
o: resigned and pessimistic
indifferent
alarmed and despairing
hopeful and practical
explanation: The last paragraph begins ‘Fortunately’, calls the problem tractable and lists affordable measures with further benefits, which is a hopeful, practical stance.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best summarises the main argument of the passage?
o: Automated systems should be banned from public decision-making
Institutions that use automated decision systems must remain accountable for the outcomes
Human officials are always fairer than machines
Automated systems are free from bias because they rely on data
explanation: The author accepts the benefits of automation but insists that ‘responsibility cannot be delegated to a machine’ and that the institution using a system must answer for its decisions.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, supporters argue that automated systems can be:
o: cheaper and more creative than human officials
entirely free of error
easier to explain than human reasoning
faster and more consistent than human officials
explanation: The first paragraph says supporters argue ‘that they can be faster and more consistent than human officials’; the passage later notes such systems can be hard to explain.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, how might an automated system come to treat certain groups unfairly?
o: By learning from past decisions that were themselves unfair
Because its designers deliberately programme prejudice into it
Because it grows tired after many decisions
Because it refuses to use past data
explanation: The second paragraph explains that a system ‘learns from past data’ and may reproduce past unfair treatment while appearing scientifically neutral.

subject: English
q: The word ‘diffused’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: made stronger
clearly assigned
spread so thinly that no one holds it
officially recorded
explanation: Responsibility is ‘diffused until no one appears to bear it’ — divided among the company, the data collector and the agency so that each can point to the others.

subject: English
q: The author’s warning that technology ‘should never become a way of escaping’ judgement implies that:
o: technology cannot assist human judgement at all
human judgement is always superior to technology
institutions may use automated systems to avoid taking responsibility for hard decisions
automated systems should review their own decisions
explanation: Having shown how responsibility can vanish among the parties behind a system, the author cautions against using automation as a shield; the same sentence says technology ‘can assist judgement’.

subject: English
q: Which of the following measures would the author support?
o: Giving affected people an intelligible reason and a review by a person
Keeping the use of automated systems secret to prevent manipulation
Making software companies alone answerable for decisions
Testing systems for unfair outcomes only after complaints arrive
explanation: The last paragraph calls for telling people when a system was involved, giving an intelligible reason and a human review, and testing systems ‘before and after they are introduced’.
